Agent swarms have the potential to drive yet another leap in output from AI. The impact will be a clear separation between teams that adopt this pattern of work and those that don’t. 

The progression has roughly been: chat gave us quick turn AI responses that let us work a bit faster, but we were still rate limited by our interactions; then agents that can go off and complete entire tasks for us, accelerating hours or days of work into minutes; to now swarms of agents that are goal seeking and will find any route to the successful completion of a project, where there’s no inherent limit to the productivity gains. 

We can imagine a future where, for any task in which value can be created within a self-contained digital environment, swarms will be able to complete the work faster than any other approach.

Essentially any area where value creation is currently bound by the amount of research you can do, the amount of decisions made with a set of software tools, the amount of data processed or consumed, and the amount of code (or code adjacent) that can be generated. 

This means swarms will play a big role in game development, coding, trading, life sciences research, IT automation, cyber, math breakthroughs, animation, and plenty of other areas of work that have these characteristics. 

There’s a lot of opportunity to build the harnesses, applied AI products, and infrastructure for how these agents operate. And most importantly there’s a ton of opportunity for those that can wire up work in this way. It’s going to be an entire new field of FDE work available.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen by @GoogleDeepMind is the fastest model in the Agent Arena top 10.

A typical Hydrogen step takes 7.3 seconds, about 2.7x faster than Claude Sonnet 5.5 and 3.1x faster than GPT-6.1 Sol.

Faster steps mean less time waiting on tasks. Across Agent Arena sessions, Hydrogen spends under 10 minutes on 82% of its tasks, compared with 55% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 44% for Claude Sonnet 5.5. Within 30 minutes, that rises to 97%, versus 81% for Sol and 78% for Sonnet 5.5.

And it isn't a quality trade-off: Hydrogen's net improvement is on par with both models.

How we measure it: A step is one model API call in an Agent Mode task. All times run from the first model request to the last streamed reply, without tool execution.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen excels at knowledge work.

Based on over 6,000 real-world agentic sessions, Hydrogen (High) is #5 in Agent Arena overall. On knowledge-work tasks, it moves up to #4.

As a result, it’s ahead of three rival models that outrank it overall: Claude Opus 5.5 (Max), GPT-6 Astra (Max) and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Max).

This means that @GoogleDeepMind's Hydrogen is not only the fastest model in the Agent Arena top 5, but also a powerful choice for real-world work.

Google's new Gemini 4 Hydrogen has Intelligence just below Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, at a third of Sonnet’s cost but ~2.5x that of GPT-6.1 Sol

@GoogleDeepMind has released their third new model in six weeks. Gemini 4 Hydrogen introduces an xhigh reasoning level and scores 54 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, with strengths in visual reasoning and non-hallucination. This places it 1 point behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max), at ~32% of Sonnet’s cost but ~2.5x that of GPT-6.1 Sol. With high reasoning, Gemini 4 Hydrogen matches the Intelligence of Gemini 4 Argon for ~19% of the Cost per Task

Key takeaways:

➤ The new xhigh reasoning level scores 54 on the Intelligence Index: xhigh is the first reasoning level above high on a Gemini model, and puts Hydrogen 1 point below Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max), and 4 points ahead of Gemini 4 Argon (high). With default (high) reasoning, Gemini 4 Hydrogen scores 51, just behind GPT-6.1 Sol (xhigh, 52) and Claude Opus 5.5 (high, 52)

➤ Strong visual reasoning, presentation and non-hallucination: On GDP.pdf, a visual reasoning benchmark over long documents, it scores 33% all-pass on medium reasoning, the tied #1 score on the benchmark. On AA-Omniscience, Hydrogen has one of the lowest hallucination rates recorded at 8%, compared with 43% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) and 52% for GPT-6.1 Sol (max). On AA-Briefcase, our agentic knowledge work evaluation, graders rate Hydrogen's presentation above other Gemini models, including Carbon

➤ Weaker on agentic terminal work: Hydrogen scores 54% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 50% on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, covering agentic coding and scientific research workflows in the terminal. Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) scores 64% and 53%, and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) scores 56% and 58%. xhigh reasoning helps on the science tasks, lifting Terminal-Bench-Science from 41% at high to 50%, but makes no difference on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (54% at both). Science scores are even across domains, from 46% in earth sciences to 53% in physical sciences

➤ Low cost for its intelligence, with high token use at xhigh: Hydrogen is priced at $1.50/$7.50 per million input/output tokens. At xhigh it costs ~32% as much per task as Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) for near-equal intelligence, but ~2.5x as much as GPT-6.1 Sol (max). xhigh nearly doubles output tokens compared with high for a 3 point gain in Intelligence, and Cost per Task falls from $3.16 at xhigh to $1.87 at high. Medium ($0.80) and low ($0.29) cost less again, but score 41 and 27 on the Intelligence Index

➤ On the Time per Task vs. Intelligence Pareto frontier: Gemini 4 Hydrogen has an output speed of ~200 output tokens per second. With high, medium, and low reasoning effort, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is on the Time per Task vs. Intelligence Pareto frontier, meaning no models are both more intelligent and have a lower Time per Task

Key model details:

➤ Context Window: 1M tokens

➤ Multimodality: Text, image, video, and speech input, with text output

➤ Reasoning efforts: Gemini 4 Hydrogen offers four reasoning levels (low, medium, high, and xhigh) with xhigh new in this release

➤ Pricing: $1.50/$7.50 per 1M input/output tokens. Cached input tokens receive a 95% discount ($0.075)

What happens to frameworks in the agents era? to component libraries? to @shadcn? 

The answer is: we need to drill deeper. Delete the part, optimize, accelerate, automate.

UI SDK is like the x86 instruction set for agents to build new UI components spontaneously. 

Agents are the new design engineers, and they're ready to build *anything* you ask, tailored to your usecase. High-level, rigid, single-framework abstractions are like kryptonite for what is essentially an infinite, untiring creation machine.

I think we've found someone that allows us to have the cake and eat it too. A decades-long dream. UI SDK is packaged behaviors that give us accessibility, performance, cohesion, saving us tokens, errors and effort, but with absolutely zero limitations and tradeoffs for what UIs we can generate.

overheard from friends talking about AI in China, and it’s very alarming

- AI short films went massive in China market because of how good the video models are now

- the first wave of people who mastered using AI to generate short films and comics made quite some money because they could produce a lot more content than traditional workflows

- but within just a few months, everybody and their mom could make equally good short films because all the expertise could be written in a markdown file

- when everyone’s more productive, no one actually has an advantage and it’s a race to the bottom. very quickly it became impossible to make money, and everyone’s busier than they were without AI

- the only one making money now is companies like bytedance who owns user demand and distribution. they sell ads to creators who pay to get traffic, and eventually ad spend became 80% of those creators’ operating expense, while AI tokens is less than 5%

so what are the problems here? 

1. there’s no moat if you are creating anything with AI

if a human is really good at something, and it’s hard to find more humans who can do the same, they can leverage the scarcity of their skill to get paid very well

but if AI is good at something, it will be infinitely replicated, so there’s no scarcity hence you can’t really expect a sustainable business by creating anything with AI

2. more creators created more content people actually liked. that’s a good thing

but the economical benefit of that all got absorbed by the distribution platforms

there’s a famous chinese poem 遍身罗绮者，不是养蚕人 - it basically says people who dress well aren’t the people making dresses. that’s exactly what’s happening here

if our society doesn’t figure out a better way to distribute wealth, AI will help billionaires become trillionaires while average people become more exhausted than ever

i found "executive mindset" to be the biggest differentiator from people who can use agents super effectively

it comes natural for people who had been an executive of a large org before, but it's counter-intuitive for people who haven't done so

a few examples

1. after you send a prompt, do you stare at the chat to see what the agent is doing?

most agent UX today leads people to do that, but a good executive never watches over an employee's shoulder after they've sent an ask - they are immediately on to the next problem

2. do you rely on chat for important decision making?

"just chat" sounds elegant, but there's a reason company executives rarely rely on plain talking for high stake decisions

instead, they ask the team for documents or presentations. it puts a bit more prep work on the team, but the discussions end up being a lot more efficient

3. when your agent did something wrong, do you curse at it and twist its arms to do it right?

some successful executives actually do that as well, but they also do something else afterwards - figure out what allowed the mistake to happen in the first place, and stop it at its root

4. do you spend all your time carefully examining everything to make sure the code is bug free?

now this is getting spicy, but you can pick any popular product on earth and you won't find a single one that's bug free

good executives accept the calculated risk and invest time in the right workflows to catch bugs early before shipping, get alerts if they happen, and making sure fixes can go out quickly - never make themselves the bottleneck by being the tester

our tools, skills, workflows etc change all the time, but building the right mindset is durable and can help you for a long time

if you aren't clear how to acquire the mindset yet, i recommend starting with asking yourself this when you try to decide to do something or not -

"if i have 100x more agents doing 100x more work for me every day, how would i do this?"

do this enough times, and you'll find yourself actually able to control 100x more agents effectively

In reasoning model development, it's always been this interesting tension between training/optimizing chain-of-thoughts (CoTs) vs not touching them to preserve monitorability.

CoTs are cool because we can check what the model is up to (e.g., whether it cheats or not) as long as it spells out its thought process. And we risk losing that if we explicitly optimize CoTs.

Two caveats:

1) I.e., the catch of CoT and monitorability is that this only works if the written thinking reflects what the model is actually doing.

2) Also, when models become more capable, they spell out less in the CoT (like a cleverer math student needs less note-taking when solving problems during an exam).

Nothing new on that front, but an interesting thread below on how to measure "harder to monitor", with some interesting results that confirm the existing intuitions:

1) no-CoT capability (meaning how much reasoning the model can do in a single forward pass without writing anything down)

- Better pretraining (lower perplexity) raises this no-CoT capability
- Architecture mostly doesn't matter
2) CoT controllability (meaning how well the model can change its written reasoning when asked to add, remove, or change parts of it)

- RL alone raises controllability a lot
- Controllability is passed on through distillation

* Higher no-CoT capability and higher controllability both make monitoring harder.

PS: Perhaps the good news is that it seems that process supervision wasn't the main culprit.
